source.title: Differences Between Hard and Noisy-labeled Samples: An Empirical Study

record.tranche_reason: The study trains networks on synthetic and real-world noisy-label datasets to develop and evaluate label-noise detection and filtering methods. It does not test whether networks fit completely random labels, how that affects training error and test error, or the learning order of true and noisy labels.
record.gate_note: The paper states that networks tend to memorize noisy labels, citing prior work, but does not report its own result measuring that behavior. Its reported filtering and test-accuracy results concern the proposed and comparison methods, not the claim’s random-label fitting behavior.
record.test_reason: The study uses training metrics to develop label-noise filtering methods. It reports neither complete random-label fitting nor clean-versus-noisy learning trajectories establishing that real patterns precede noise memorization. Accuracy averaged over training does not establish that temporal order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors propose controlled hardness transformations and combine static centroid distance with accuracy over training to filter noisy examples while retaining hard examples. They conclude that this improves downstream generalization and can support semi-supervised learning. They do not establish a new result on complete random-label fitting or real-before-noise memorization.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains image classifiers on datasets with controlled, class-dependent hardness and label-noisiness levels, then evaluates sample metrics and filtering methods. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Hardness type changes the metric behavior; the study reports that some metrics vary with certain hardness types as they do with noisiness, while SCD does not show that pattern.

fits_no_version.finding: Loss rises and confidence falls with increasing noisiness and hardness; several other metrics, including accuracy averaged over training, also respond similarly to both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Common sample metrics can confound correctly labeled hard examples with mislabeled examples in these synthetic image-classification settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Static centroid distance increases with noisiness without the corresponding increase with hardness shown by other metrics.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Static centroid distance helps distinguish hard clean examples from mislabeled examples in the tested settings.

record.problems: The synthetic hardness and noise settings are controlled constructions; the authors state that their hardness approaches do not cover all contexts in which hard samples arise. The reported sample-metric trends do not directly measure memorization or fitting error on random labels.
record.rows_left_out: Filtering-method comparisons and test accuracies on filtered datasets (Tables 1–4) evaluate dataset partitioning and downstream training, not the claim’s random-label fitting behavior. No rows were omitted for a directly tested claim version.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error and chance test performance with completely random labels under unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true and random labels, and convergence slowdown across corruption fractions.
Perfect fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily increasing test error across corruption fractions from none to all.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Temporal evidence that shared real patterns are learned before noisy labels are memorized.

record.verdict_notes: The qualitative metric trends are reported observations, but their states are cannot_determine relative to the supplied claim versions. Lower accuracy averaged over training can reflect delayed learning, persistent failure, or both; it does not establish later memorization. No additional result directly bearing on a claim version is missing from the record.

versions.untested_parts: Whether standard networks fit completely random labels with near-zero training error and chance test error without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Training-time cost of fitting random labels and convergence as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and test-error behavior across corruption levels from none to all.
Whether regularization, dropout, or augmentation affect random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels, and whether those labels are learned differently over training.

rows.subject: MobileNetV2
rows.operation_detail: Measured sample loss and confidence across synthetic noisiness and hardness levels.

conditions.value: noisiness level n; maximum label noise 40%
hardness level h; three hardness types

rows.measure: Training loss and prediction confidence by noisiness level.
rows.value: As noisiness increases, loss increases and confidence decreases; the same direction of change occurs as hardness increases.
rows.note: This measures sample-level metrics, not training error or generalization for random labels.
rows.check: Loss and confidence trends cannot establish any claim version. The subject is incomplete: the decision-boundary hardness experiments use ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121, whereas imbalance and diversification use MobileNetV2. The maximum replacement probability is 40%; labels are randomized within classes sharing the same noisiness level.

source_check.correct: Loss increases and confidence decreases with noisiness, as with hardness. The imbalance and diversification experiments use randomly initialized MobileNetV2; the decision-boundary experiments use ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121. Loss and confidence are measured at the end of training.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.4; Figure 3 caption; Section 3.3; Section 2 metric definitions; Appendix A, experimental setup for each hardness type.
source_check.problem: MobileNetV2 alone incorrectly describes the models used across all three hardness types.

rows.subject: MobileNetV2
rows.operation_detail: Compared feature-distance metrics across synthetic noisiness and hardness levels.

conditions.value: hardness level h; three hardness types

rows.measure: Static centroid distance (SCD) and adaptive centroid distance (ACD).
rows.value: SCD increases with noisiness but not with hardness; ACD is monotonic in both noisiness and hardness.
rows.note: This is a feature-metric result used for sample partitioning, not a test of random-label fitting.
rows.check: Centroid distances do not measure random-label fitting or learning order. The decision-boundary condition uses pretrained DenseNet121, not MobileNetV2. SCD is measured when training accuracy first reaches 50%; ACD is measured at training end.

source_check.correct: SCD increases with noisiness but not hardness; ACD is monotonic in both. The imbalance and diversification experiments use MobileNetV2; the decision-boundary experiments use ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121. SCD is computed at the first epoch with training accuracy at least 50%; ACD is computed at the end of training.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 4 caption; Section 4.1; Section 2, ACD and SCD definitions; Appendix A.
source_check.problem: The decision-boundary results belong to ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121, not MobileNetV2.

rows.subject: MobileNetV2
rows.operation_detail: Compared sample metrics as synthetic hardness and noisiness levels varied.

conditions.value: imbalance, diversification, and closeness to decision boundary

rows.measure: Loss, confidence, accuracy over training, AUL, AUM, JSD, and ACD trends.
rows.value: The metrics are monotonic with noisiness and with at least one hardness type; SCD does not show the same trend with hardness as with noisiness.
rows.note: The paper describes metric trends for distinguishing sample types; it does not report a random-label training-error result.
rows.check: These aggregate metrics do not establish perfect fitting, convergence time, or real-before-noise learning order. Accuracy over training is a temporal average, not a trajectory. The decision-boundary condition uses pretrained DenseNet121, not MobileNetV2.

source_check.correct: The listed metrics change monotonically with noisiness and show the same direction of change for at least one hardness type; SCD distinguishes these changes. The imbalance and diversification experiments use MobileNetV2; the decision-boundary experiments use ImageNet-pretrained DenseNet121. Accuracy over training is the per-sample average of prediction correctness across epochs.
source_check.locator_found: Appendix B, Comparison to Other Metrics; Figure 6 caption; Appendix A; Section 2, Accuracy of Predictions over Training definition.
source_check.problem: The combined result spans two architectures; MobileNetV2 does not cover the decision-boundary condition.

relation.reason: The study develops filtering methods using training-derived metrics without testing complete random-label fitting, optimization cost, unstructured-input fitting, perfect fitting across noise levels, regularization claims or real-before-noise learning order.

tranche.reason: The paper uses noisy-label memorization as motivation for label-noise detection and reports sample metrics, filtering performance and downstream generalization. Its results do not establish any listed claim version.

source_check.notes: The synthetic experiments use a maximum label-replacement probability of 40%, varying by class. Aggregate accuracy over training and centroid-distance trends do not establish memorization order; cannot_determine and the absence of version verdicts are appropriate.
